passages.title: Personality Traits Vs Position In Family
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 3: "Personality Traits Vs Position In Family"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: Part 3. You will hear two students, Ruth and Ed, preparing a presentation about birth order and personality. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 26.
[00:54] RUTH: Ed, how are you progressing with the reading for our presentation next week?
[00:59] ED: Reasonably well, Ruth, although there's an enormous amount to get through.
[01:05] RUTH: I know. I hadn't realized that birth order had attracted so much research.

[01:11] ED: Most of what I've found about birth order and personality isn't very dependable. Many claims that a person's place in the family produces particular traits seem to be stereotypes rather than conclusions supported by strong evidence.
[01:29] RUTH: That itself could make a useful opening point. We could first summarize what earlier studies reported. Some of them go back more than a century.

[01:41] ED: All right. We could review the traits they commonly suggested. For example, oldest children were often described as less emotionally settled because they never fully adjusted when a younger child arrived.

[01:56] RUTH: On the positive side, several studies portrayed them as caring. In the past, when families were larger, the eldest would often have been responsible for looking after younger brothers and sisters.
[02:11] ED: The evidence about middle children is less consistent, but many studies say they tend to be cooperative and easier to live with than either the oldest or the youngest.

[02:23] RUTH: They're supposed to be helpful and keen to please. That certainly doesn't describe my middle brother, though. He was extremely difficult, always starting arguments and resenting anything I had.

[02:38] ED: These descriptions don't match my experience either. I'm the youngest, and the research says I should have been outgoing and confident, making friends easily. In reality, I was painfully shy.
[02:53] RUTH: Really? That's interesting. There are hundreds of twin studies, although most examine the relative effects of upbringing and genetics.
[03:03] ED: I found one about personality. It suggested that twins are often introverted in social settings because each can rely on the other for support.
[03:14] RUTH: My cousins behaved like that as children. They focused almost entirely on one another and struggled to mix with other children, although they're fine now.

[03:26] ED: Only children have often been judged very negatively. A lot of research labels them selfish loners who assume everything should center on them because they never compete for parental attention.

[03:39] RUTH: That sounds rather unfair. Another group I hadn't considered was children whose siblings are much older. A few studies say these children become independent earlier because they are expected to manage basic tasks, such as dressing themselves.
[03:57] ED: That's plausible, although some might do the opposite and act like the baby of the family, constantly seeking special attention.
[04:08] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30.
[04:54] RUTH: What do you think was the main weakness in many of those studies?
[04:59] ED: Often the researchers collected information from just one child in each family. That child assessed both themselves and all their siblings, so the academic results have held up though.
[05:19] RUTH: Intelligence test scores tend to fall slightly from the eldest child to each younger sibling, and recent studies have repeatedly found the same pattern.

[05:30] ED: Yes, but many researchers failed to account for family size. Families with more children are more likely to have a lower socioeconomic status. And that can also explain differences in academic performance.
[05:46] RUTH: For instance, an oldest son might receive opportunities that his younger sisters do not.
[05:54] ED: Exactly.

[05:55] RUTH: What surprises me is the principal explanation for the oldest child's slightly better academic results. Extraparental attention in early childhood provides an intellectual advantage, which I expected. But the more unexpected benefit comes from teaching younger siblings and having to put processes into words.

[06:19] ED: Yes, and acting as a teacher gives the eldest child status and confidence, which can also make a small contribution to achievement. Do you feel that rivalry with your siblings benefited you?

[06:32] RUTH: I think it did. My younger brother was incredibly irritating and we argued constantly, but that taught me to stand up for myself. I would never have apologized to him after our worst disagreements, yet we had to tolerate one another and usually managed to live together quite peacefully.
[06:53] ED: My experience was similar. Having two older brothers certainly didn't teach me to share. I never wanted them using my possessions.
[07:04] RUTH: That seems perfectly normal, whereas...
[07:07] NARRATOR: That is the end of part three. You now have one minute to check your answers to part three.

passages.title: The Eucalyptus Tree In Australia
content: 📌 The Eucalyptus tree in Australia

Why the tree is important
• It supplies [ _____ ] and food to many different species.
• Its leaves yield [ _____ ], which is an ingredient in disinfectant.
Why eucalyptus numbers are currently falling
A) Diseases

(i) Mundulla Yellows
Cause:
• Lime used during the construction of [ _____ ] entered the ground.
• The roots could no longer absorb the iron the trees required.

(ii) Bell-miner Associated Die-back
Cause:
• [ _____ ] consume the eucalyptus foliage.
• They produce a sugary substance.
• Bell-miner birds seek this substance and drive other species away.

B) Bushfires — William Jackson’s theory
• Very frequent fires alter the vegetation and lead to the spread of [ _____ ].
• Fires occurring at a moderate frequency encourage eucalyptus forest because they:
  • leave more [ _____ ] for eucalyptus trees;
  • preserve the condition of the [ _____ ].
• When fires are rare, “[ _____ ] rainforest” develops. This is:
  • a [ _____ ] ecosystem;
  • an ideal place for bell-miners to build their [ _____ ].
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: Part 4. You will hear part of a lecture about eucalyptus trees in Australia and the threats they currently face. First, you have some time to look at questions 31-40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31-40.

[00:53] AUDIO: Today's subject is the eucalyptus, one of Australia's most familiar trees and also widely known as the gum tree. I'll begin by explaining its importance before examining several problems that are now affecting it. Eucalyptus trees matter for many reasons. They provide shelter for animals such as bats and birds, while numerous species also obtain food from them, especially nectar from their flowers.

[01:24] AUDIO: They therefore make an important contribution to biodiversity. The trees are useful to people as well. Oil taken from eucalyptus leaves is an ingredient in a disinfectant that destroys germs. These trees grow throughout Australia and may survive for as long as four centuries.

[01:46] AUDIO: It is therefore worrying that eucalyptus numbers are declining across the country because many trees are dying much earlier than they should. What is causing this? Disease is one possible explanation. In the 1970s, trees began to develop a condition known as mandula yellows.

[02:09] AUDIO: Their leaves slowly became yellow and the trees eventually died. Researchers did not identify the cause until 2004. Lime, whose chemical name is calcium hydroxide, had been used to construct roads. Rain carried it into the surrounding ground, where it affected the roots of nearby eucalyptus trees and prevented them from absorbing the iron necessary for healthy growth.

[02:40] AUDIO: When iron was injected back into the affected trees, they recovered immediately. Mandula yellows damaged only a fairly limited number of trees. By 2000, however, vast areas of eucalyptus along Australia's east coast were being affected by bell miner-associated dieback. This disease is often found where large populations of bell miner birds live and, again, the leaves suffer the damage.

[03:10] AUDIO: Insects settle on the foliage and feed on it, destroying the leaves as they move around. At the same time, they release a sugary substance. Bell miners are strongly attracted to it and drive away other species that might compete for it. The birds and insects then multiply at the expense of other wildlife until the leaves are so badly damaged that the tree dies.

[03:38] AUDIO: Specialists have noticed that eucalyptus trees may appear unhealthy before bell miner-associated dieback becomes visible, so another factor may be involved. One possibility concerns Australia's extensive bushfires. More than 40 years ago, ecologist William Jackson proposed that the frequency of fires in a region determines the vegetation that follows. Very frequent fires encourage grass to take over, whereas moderately frequent fires favor eucalyptus forest.

[04:15] AUDIO: Why can fairly regular burning support eucalyptus? First, fire limits competing plants that would otherwise use the water required by the trees. It also prevents quick-growing bushes and other vegetation from changing the soil and removing its nutrients. Some bushfires are therefore necessary for eucalyptus survival, provided they do not occur too often.

[04:42] AUDIO: There is evidence that Indigenous Australians deliberately burned areas of bush at regular intervals for thousands of years before Europeans arrived. Since European settlement, bushfires have been tightly controlled. Scientists now think that reducing them to a very low frequency has encouraged the development of what is called dry rainforest. The name sounds unusual because rainforest is commonly associated with wet conditions.

[05:14] AUDIO: Unlike a species-rich tropical rainforest, this is a simple ecosystem. Its vegetation is thick and dense but contains little variety. The heavy shade creates an ideal habitat for one particular species, the bell-minor bird, which builds its nest in the undergrowth. That, once again, is harmful to eucalyptus trees.
[05:45] AUDIO: That is the end of part four. You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.

transcript: [00:01] NARRATOR: Part 1. You will hear Jean phoning a tourist information office about a local festival. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 4. Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 4.
[00:53] TIM: Good morning, tourist information office. Tim speaking. What can I do for you?
[00:59] JEAN: Hello, my family and I are visiting next month and I was hoping you could tell me about the festival taking place while we're there.
[01:07] TIM: Certainly. The program begins on the afternoon of the 17th with a concert.
[01:13] JEAN: Is that the orchestra and choir from the United States?
[01:18] TIM: Not quite. They're Canadian. They're very well known at home and they'll perform familiar pieces that should suit both adults and children.
[01:28] JEAN: Excellent. We all enjoy live music.
[01:32] TIM: Then on the 18th, a ballet company called Eustatus will perform.
[01:38] JEAN: Could you spell the name for me?
[01:40] TIM: Of course. E-U-S-T-A-T-I-S. They were here last year and the audience loved them. This year's production is suitable for every age group as well.
[01:55] JEAN: We'll probably book that. Is there a play too? A comedy would be ideal.
[02:03] TIM: Yes. A local amateur company is presenting Jemima on the afternoons of the 19th and 20th. One of its members wrote it. They've staged it a few times already.
[02:16] TIM: And although I haven't seen it, the newspaper review was extremely positive.
[02:22] JEAN: Would young children enjoy it?
[02:24] TIM: They should. It's actually aimed more at children than adults, which is why both performances are in the afternoon.
[02:34] JEAN: What about anything involving dance?
[02:37] TIM: There's a dance show on the evening of the 20th. A professional company will perform modern pieces accompanied by electronic music from young composers.
[02:49] JEAN: I see.
[02:50] TIM: The production explores the ways people communicate, and sometimes fail to. So it has the slightly unusual title, Chat.
[03:00] JEAN: That makes sense. People chat in person as well as online.
[03:04] TIM: Exactly.
[03:08] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions five to ten. Now listen and answer questions five to ten.
[03:53] TIM: There are workshops and outdoor activities as well. Each is offered at least once a day, so nobody should miss out.
[04:01] JEAN: We're especially keen on cooking. Is there a cookery session?
[04:06] TIM: Yes. It shows how food can form part of a healthy way of life. Even cakes can be prepared with far less sugar than usual.
[04:16] JEAN: That sounds useful. We're trying to get the children more interested in cooking.

[04:21] TIM: There's another workshop exclusively for children. They'll design posters showing the town's history and how daily life has changed over the centuries. Their work will later be displayed at the community center. The third workshop is only for adults and involves making toys.
[04:44] JEAN: Why can't children join that one?
[04:46] TIM: Because it's a carpentry session. The toys are made from wood, and participants will use sharp chisels and several other tools.
[04:58] JEAN: Then keeping it adult only is sensible.
[05:01] TIM: But we thought so. Outdoors, there will be supervised wild swimming.
[05:07] JEAN: What exactly does wild swimming mean?
[05:10] TIM: Swimming in natural water rather than a pool.
[05:13] JEAN: So somewhere like a lake?
[05:15] TIM: Yes. A lovely lake just beyond the town will be used, with lifeguards present. So all ages can take part. There'll also be a daily walk through the nearby woods.
[05:29] TIM: The guide specializes in insects and will point out different species and explain their importance to the environment.
[05:37] JEAN: There's certainly plenty to choose from.
[05:40] TIM: If you want updates on the preparations, the festival organizer is writing a blog. You'll find it through the festival website.
[05:50] JEAN: Thanks very much. That's been really helpful.
[05:52] TIM: You're welcome. Goodbye.
[05:54] JEAN: Goodbye.
[05:57] NARRATOR: That is the end of part one. You now have one minute to check your answers to part one.

transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a guest speaker describing the history and recent redevelopment of Minster Park. First, you have some time to look at questions 11-14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11-14. I'm delighted to introduce our speaker this evening, Mark Logan, who will talk about the changes recently made to Minster Park.

[00:58] AUDIO: Mark, please begin. Oh, thank you. Most of you know Minster Park, which has existed for well over a hundred years and has usually been managed by the City Council. Its beginnings are less familiar.

[01:14] AUDIO: Many public parks were once gardens attached to grand private houses. But Minster was different. In 1892, local residents began planting flowers on an unused piece of ground, whose ownership was uncertain. The Council did not formally acquire the land until 20 years later.

[01:40] AUDIO: You may have seen the statue close to one of the entrances. It represents Diane Gosforth, an important figure in the park's history. After taking legal possession, the Council intended to sell the site for housing, but local residents wanted to keep it as a public green space. Especially because the surrounding neighbourhood was already densely built up.

[02:07] AUDIO: Gosforth led petitions and public demonstrations, and the campaign eventually persuaded the Council to abandon the sale. The First World War began soon afterwards, in 1914. Most of the park was then dug over for growing vegetables, which were sold within the area. The Army did consider using the park for military exercises and even contacted the Council, but decided that the site was too small.

[02:39] AUDIO: A section of grass remained available for occasional public meetings. After the war, the park was largely restored to its earlier appearance and changed very little for decades. New plans were prepared several times, including a scheme in 2013. That proposal was altered in 2015, before construction began.

[03:06] AUDIO: The actual transformation started in 2016 and was completed on time last year. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20. Now I'll describe what has changed and what remains.

[04:02] AUDIO: On the map, the river marks the northern edge of the park, while the other three walls each contain a gate. Diane Gosforth's statue has been relocated. It once stood near the south gate, but is now directly north of the Lily Pond, close to the centre, where visitors can see it more easily. A new collection of wooden sculptures has been installed beside the river, at the sharp bend in the path coming from the east gate.

[04:36] AUDIO: Two sections are mainly for children. The larger improved playground lies between the river and the path running north from the pond. The second is a new circular maze formed by low hedges. Starting at the west gate, walk north towards the river and turn left to reach it.

[04:58] AUDIO: The long-established tennis courts have increased from four to eight. They remain in the southwest corner, beside the right-angled turn in the path. Finally, the new fitness area is immediately next to the Lily Pond, on the same side as the west gate. Now I'd like to move on to the planting scheme.

content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 3: "Cathy And Graham"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: Part 3. You will hear two students, Kathy and Graham, planning a university display about 19th century British life and literature. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24.
[00:55] CATHY: Right, Graham. Let's make sure we've both understood the assignment.
[01:00] GRAHAM: Good idea.
[01:02] CATHY: For the university open day, we need to plan a display about British society and literature in the middle of the 19th century.
[01:11] GRAHAM: Yes. Other people will locate the materials and assemble everything. At this stage, our job is simply to produce the plan.
[01:21] CATHY: Do you know who the display is meant to attract? I couldn't tell whether the main audience was English students or people studying other subjects.

[01:31] GRAHAM: That was the arrangement in previous years, but hardly anyone attended. This time, it's part of an open day intended to improve the university's profile. It will be advertised across the city so local residents can see what happens here, and details are being sent to people who may apply to study next year.
[01:54] CATHY: Current students and teaching staff will probably visit as well, won't they?
[01:59] GRAHAM: Probably, but we've specifically been asked to focus on those other two groups.
[02:04] CATHY: Fine. We don't have to represent every 19th century writer, do we?
[02:10] GRAHAM: No. The choice is ours. Why don't we base the whole display on Charles Dickens?

[02:17] CATHY: That would work. His name and novels are still widely recognized, and many people have watched screen adaptations even if they haven't read the books. He gives us an accessible way into the period.
[02:32] GRAHAM: Exactly. His fiction also exposed the terrible living conditions faced by much of the population. He hoped that drawing attention to those problems would push society to respond.
[02:46] CATHY: Did he campaign in any other ways?
[02:49] GRAHAM: He supported education and other reforms and delivered public speeches. But I think we should leave those activities aside and concentrate on what he published.
[03:01] CATHY: Agreed.
[03:04] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30.
[03:50] CATHY: Shall we now match one aspect of Victorian life with each novel?
[03:55] GRAHAM: Yes. I've brought a chronological list of the novels, assuming you'd accept my Dickens idea.
[04:02] CATHY: Fortunately for you, I did. The Pickwick Papers came first, in 1836. It sold extremely well and was adapted for the stage almost immediately.
[04:16] GRAHAM: There's another useful detail. One character repeatedly falls asleep, and a medical disorder was later named Pickwickian Syndrome after the book.
[04:28] CATHY: Perfect. Let's make medicine the theme and support it with quotations.
[04:33] GRAHAM: Next comes Oliver Twist. Poverty is an obvious possibility, but perhaps we can choose something less predictable.
[04:42] CATHY: Oliver is trained to steal instead of going to school. We could use that to show how few poor children received formal education and how they learned elsewhere.
[04:53] GRAHAM: Good. Which book follows?
[04:57] CATHY: Nicholas Nickleby, perhaps. Nicholas teaches at an appalling school.
[05:02] GRAHAM: True, but he also joins a travelling theatre company. Let's use the book to explore theatre and other forms of entertainment, so the display isn't entirely about hardship.
[05:15] CATHY: Alright.
[05:16] GRAHAM: In Martin Chuzlewit, the main character travels to the United States, doesn't he?
[05:22] CATHY: Yes. And Dickens himself had visited America the previous year, so his own journey influenced the novel.
[05:30] GRAHAM: The book also deals strongly with selfishness, which could lead into social justice. Actually, that's too broad. Your travel idea is more focused, so we'll keep it.
[05:43] CATHY: Bleak House was next, and it's the one I like best.
[05:47] GRAHAM: Mine too. Its attack on the legal system is extremely sharp.

[05:52] CATHY: It is, but Esther's experiences might offer a better theme. She is treated badly by the woman she later discovers is her aunt, becomes happy while managing her guardian's household, and eventually marries and receives a home of her own.
[06:11] GRAHAM: Yes, that gives us a clear account of a woman's life.
[06:15] CATHY: Then we could use little Dorrit. Mr. Dorrit spends years in a debtor's prison.
[06:21] GRAHAM: Like Dickens's father, I think.
[06:24] CATHY: That's right.
[06:24] GRAHAM: What if we concentrate on the moment Mr. Dorrit inherits a fortune and begins behaving as though he has always belonged to the wealthy classes?
[06:35] CATHY: Good choice. Now we need to decide what material will illustrate each theme, and that may be the difficult part.
[06:46] NARRATOR: That is the end of part three. You now have one minute to check your answers to part three.

content: 📌 Agricultural programme in Mozambique
How the programme was organised

The project operated in a dry part of Chicualacuala district near the Limpopo River.Local families relied on charcoal from the forest for income.[ _____ ] was treated as the main priority for securing a water supply.[ _____ ] carried out most of the work organised by the farmers’ associations.Fenced plots protected crops from animals.
The programme supplied:
[ _____ ] for constructing the fences[ _____ ] for crops suited to local conditionswater pumps
The farmers supplied:
labour[ _____ ] to support the fences on their land
Further developments

Selling produce was sometimes difficult because [ _____ ] was unavailable.Farmers therefore received training in food [ _____ ].Special tanks were built where [ _____ ] could be raised.Local residents later proposed keeping [ _____ ].
Evaluation and lessons learned
Higher agricultural output improved income and food security.Realistic schedules are essential, particularly during the [ _____ ] phase.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: Part 4. You will hear part of a lecture about an agricultural development program in Mozambique. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

[00:52] AUDIO: Today I'll discuss a case study of a program designed to support rural communities in Mozambique, a country in the Southeast Africa where agriculture is central to many people's lives. The work involved three communities in Chiklakwala district close to the Limpopo River. Rainfall in this dry region is unreliable, so farming alone could not provide a living. Instead, residents earned money from the forest, mainly by producing and selling charcoal, because the forest was being depleted quickly however, this could not continue indefinitely.

[01:34] AUDIO: The first priority was to use water already available in the Limpopo River. Irrigation systems were established to give crops and livestock a dependable supply. The program and the district government worked together on implementation. One farmers association already existed and two more were formed.

[01:56] AUDIO: They organized water management, animal breeding, and crop production with women carrying out most of the work. To stop wild and domestic animals damaging crops, the communities enclosed special cultivation areas. Local people built the fences while the program supplied the wire needed for them. After the land had been protected, it was prepared for vegetables and cereals suited to the climate.

[02:25] AUDIO: The program provided the seeds together with pumps and pipes to move river water to the fields. Residents contributed all the labor and also supplied and installed the posts supporting the fences on their own land. Once the scheme was operating, its progress was monitored. Farmers produced more than their households required and could sell the surplus.

[02:52] AUDIO: Reaching markets was sometimes difficult however, because transport was unavailable. Considerable quantities, particularly vegetables, spoiled before they could be sold. The associations therefore agreed that farmers should be trained in food preservation techniques. A further activity developed even though it had not appeared in the original plan.

[03:17] AUDIO: Farmers dug tanks inside the fenced areas, filled them with water and used them to raise fish, providing an important source of protein. Later, local residents proposed keeping bees. This idea was also adopted with honey produced both for household use and for sale. What can we learn from the program?

[03:40] AUDIO: In dry regions with reliable access to water, agriculture can have substantial potential. Production in Chikawala-Kawala rose markedly, improving both household income and food security. Yet schedules must be realistic for every stage, especially the design phase, because errors made then may be difficult to correct later. Overall, the case shows that sustainable development can be achieved in places where that is the end of part four.
[04:20] AUDIO: You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.

passages.title: Employment Agency: Possible Jobs
content: 📌 Employment Agency: Possible Jobs

First job
Administrative assistant for a North London company that makes [ _____ ]

Duties
• entering data
• attending [ _____ ] and recording notes
• general office administration
• looking after the [ _____ ]

Skills required
• strong computer ability, especially spreadsheets
• effective people skills
• careful attention to [ _____ ]

Experience
• at least [ _____ ] of teleconferencing experience

Second job
Warehouse assistant in South London

Duties
• controlling stock
• organising [ _____ ]

Skills required
• confident with numbers
• competent with computers
• highly organised and [ _____ ]
• good spoken and written communication
• comfortable working in a [ _____ ]
• able to handle [ _____ ] goods

Previous experience needed
• driving in London
• warehouse work
• [ _____ ] service
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear a job agency advisor discussing two possible vacancies with a candidate. First, you have some time to look at questions one to five. Now listen carefully and answer questions one to five.
[00:53] SALLY: Good morning, Joe. Thanks for coming into the agency. I'm Sally Baker, one of the advisors here.
[01:00] JOE: Hello, Sally. We spoke by phone earlier, didn't we?
[01:03] SALLY: Yes, that's right. Thanks for sending your CV. We've reviewed it carefully and found two vacancies that could be a good match.
[01:14] JOE: Great.
[01:15] SALLY: The first is with a firm in north London. They need an administrative assistant.
[01:21] JOE: What kind of business is it?
[01:23] SALLY: It's called Home Solutions. The company designs and manufactures furniture.
[01:30] JOE: That's not an industry I know much about. But it sounds interesting.
[01:36] SALLY: The role is office-based, and your previous work covers several of the things they need. Your CV says you've done data entry.
[01:46] JOE: Yes, quite a lot.
[01:48] SALLY: Good. The successful applicant will also attend meetings and make notes during them.
[01:55] JOE: I've done that before too.
[01:57] SALLY: There will be routine administrative work as well.
[02:00] JOE: Things like filing and maintaining records? That's fine. In my last post, I was also responsible for the diary.
[02:09] SALLY: Excellent. Diary management is on their list too. You should add that to your CV because I don't think it appears there.
[02:18] JOE: No, I left it out.
[02:20] SALLY: As for the requirements, strong computer skills are essential, particularly using spreadsheets.
[02:28] JOE: That won't be a problem.
[02:30] SALLY: They also want good interpersonal skills, which they would probably confirm through your referees.
[02:37] JOE: That should be fine.
[02:39] SALLY: They emphasise being accurate as well, someone who pays close attention to detail. From the way your CV is presented, I'd say you meet that requirement.
[02:52] JOE: I think so. Is any particular experience necessary?
[02:56] SALLY: They ask for previous experience of teleconferencing.
[03:00] JOE: I've been doing that for three years.
[03:03] SALLY: That's more than enough. Their minimum is one year. Would you consider applying?
[03:09] JOE: Yes. Although North London would mean a fairly long journey to work.
[03:14] SALLY: I understand.
[03:17] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.
[04:04] SALLY: In that case, the second vacancy may be better located for you. It's a warehouse assistant job in South London.
[04:13] JOE: That would be much nearer.
[04:15] SALLY: And you've worked in a warehouse previously, correct?
[04:18] JOE: Yes.
[04:19] SALLY: The main duties are controlling stock and organising deliveries.
[04:23] JOE: I can handle that. You need to monitor everything carefully, and I've always been comfortable with figures.
[04:31] SALLY: Good. Working confidently with numbers is their first requirement. They also need someone with solid computer skills, which you have.
[04:42] JOE: Certainly.
[04:43] SALLY: Next, they mention organisational ability. The person must be very well organised.
[04:50] JOE: I'd say I am.
[04:51] SALLY: And tidy?
[04:53] JOE: Yes. In a warehouse, those qualities really go together.
[04:58] SALLY: They also expect clear communication, both spoken and written.
[05:04] JOE: Fine. One thing I especially liked in my last warehouse job was working as part of a team. That was essential.
[05:13] SALLY: That's useful because they specifically want someone accustomed to team-working. What products did you handle in your last warehouse?
[05:23] JOE: Mainly bathroom and kitchen equipment, sinks, cookers and refrigerators.
[05:29] SALLY: So, lifting heavy goods is alright for you?
[05:33] JOE: Yes. I'm strong enough and I've completed the appropriate training.
[05:38] SALLY: Excellent. In terms of experience, they require a driving licence and familiarity with driving in London traffic.
[05:49] JOE: That's no problem.
[05:51] SALLY: You already have warehouse experience, and the last thing they ask for is customer service. Your CV shows suitable experience there too.
[06:01] JOE: Good. Could you tell me something about the salary?
[06:07] NARRATOR: That is the end of part one. You now have one minute to check your answers to part one.

passages.title: Street Play Scheme
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "Street Play Scheme"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: Part 2 You will hear a radio presenter interviewing a woman who helped establish a street play scheme. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 16. My guest today is Alice Riches, who set up the street play scheme in Beechwood Road where she lives.

[01:02] AUDIO: If you haven't heard of street play, residents close their road for a few hours so children can play outside safely. Alice began with her own street, and similar schemes now operate across the city. Alice, when did yours actually begin? The idea first occurred to me when my oldest child was a toddler, roughly six years ago, but campaigning took more than two years before we could put it into practice, so the scheme has actually been running for three years.

[01:40] AUDIO: Ideally, we'd close the road for an entire weekend, from Saturday morning to Sunday evening. At present, it happens once a week. When we first started, it was only monthly. What happens when Beechwood Road is closed?

[01:59] AUDIO: Volunteer wardens stand at both ends of the road. Most are parents, although some older residents help as well. The council supplied special signs, and a volunteer explains the arrangement to drivers. Most motorists are reasonable, and we've only needed police assistance once or twice.

[02:20] AUDIO: The road isn't totally closed to vehicles. Residents may still drive in or out, provided they stay below 20 kilometers an hour. Most decide not to drive at all, or leave their cars in a nearby street. The warden's main job is to prevent through traffic.

[02:40] AUDIO: Can any neighborhood apply to take part? Definitely. We want children throughout the city to be included, especially those living beside busy roads, because that is where the need is greatest. Demand is naturally lower in affluent districts, where children often have large gardens or parks, and in quieter suburbs with more outdoor space.

[03:07] AUDIO: I'd encourage anyone interested to try it. The response from residents across the city has been overwhelmingly positive, including people without children. A very small number complain, but most say they enjoy seeing children using the street, even though the games can be noisy. Before you hear the rest of the interview, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20.

[04:09] AUDIO: Now listen and answer questions 17 to 20. Street play has brought children many benefits. Parents appreciate that they are outdoors in fresh air instead of looking at a screen, even when the games are not especially energetic. Playing with friends without constant adult supervision is valuable too.

[04:36] AUDIO: For me, the main benefit is that children gain confidence in being outside independently. Equally important, they get to know the adults living nearby, so the street begins to feel like one large family. Those are considerable benefits. I'd now like to ask about the related experiment in King Street.

[04:59] AUDIO: King Street is the busiest main road locally, and residents wanted to reduce its traffic for one day by encouraging people to leave their cars at home. We considered increasing parking charges, but that would have been very unpopular. Instead, parking was prohibited on King Street while the other car park stayed open. The impact was remarkable.

[05:25] AUDIO: We expected the air to be cleaner, and it was. What surprised me was the reduction in noise, even though buses continued to run. People also reported feeling safer. The biggest shock was that shop sales rose substantially.

[05:44] AUDIO: We had assumed fewer people would come out to shop, not more. That's fascinating. So the fact that that is the end of part two. You now have one minute to check your answers to part two.

passages.title: Hazel Analysed Items In Newspapers
content: 📌 Hazel analysed items in newspapers

Features Hazel should examine in newspaper items
• the [ _____ ] where the item appears
• the item’s [ _____ ], including its headline
• any [ _____ ] presented with the text
• the item’s [ _____ ], including which material receives emphasis
• the writer’s main [ _____ ]
• any [ _____ ] the writer makes about the audience
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: Part 3. You will hear two students discussing a media studies assignment on newspaper coverage. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 26.
[00:52] HAZEL: Tom, could I get some advice from you?
[00:56] TOM: Of course, if I can help. What do you need to know?
[00:58] HAZEL: It's about my first media studies assignment. I'm uncertain how to approach it and I know you completed the same task last year.
[01:08] TOM: Is that the assignment where you compare how several newspapers report the same story?
[01:13] HAZEL: Yes, exactly.
[01:15] TOM: I remember it. I really enjoyed that piece of work.
[01:20] HAZEL: What features should I compare?
[01:22] TOM: There are quite a few. Begin by noting which page each newspaper puts the item on.
[01:28] HAZEL: Because a story on the front page is treated very differently from one place near the bottom of page 10?
[01:36] TOM: Precisely. Its position indicates the importance the editor gives it. Then examine the size, the number of column inches and how many columns the item occupies.
[01:48] HAZEL: That would include the headline as well, I suppose.
[01:52] TOM: Certainly. The headline is a major part of catching a reader's eye.
[01:55] HAZEL: Should I also check the graphics? Any photographs or other visual material alongside the writing?

[02:03] TOM: Yes. Visual elements can strongly influence how a reader understands a story, sometimes more than the words. You should also analyze the structure, how the item has been organized. Since many people read only the opening paragraph, consider which information the journalist puts first.
[02:27] TOM: If there are opposing views, notice whether one is left until near the end, where fewer readers will see it.
[02:35] HAZEL: Newspapers can also publish inaccurate or misleading information, either intentionally or by mistake. Should I investigate that?

[02:45] TOM: If possible, compare the different accounts and try to establish what is reliable. That leads to another essential issue, the writer's main purpose. An article may appear simply to inform, but it may actually aim to provoke fear, start controversy, or make a person seem ridiculous.
[03:06] HAZEL: I understand. And writers probably make assumptions about their readers, too.

[03:13] TOM: Exactly. Assumptions about what readers already know, their attitudes, and their education. The writing has to be understandable without sounding patronizing. All of those factors affect the presentation of the story.
[03:31] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30.
[04:16] HAZEL: Does it make any difference what category of story I choose?

[04:21] TOM: Not really. It could be national or international politics, the arts, or almost anything, provided two or three newspapers have covered it. Naturally, the work will be easier and more enjoyable if you already know and care about the subject.
[04:38] HAZEL: Then a national news story sounds worthwhile. I'm interested in politics. So I'll definitely search for an appropriate one. What subject did you analyze?

[04:50] TOM: I wanted to compare editorials because I was interested in the way newspapers state their opinions openly. But I couldn't find two editorials on the same issue that I actually wanted to examine.
[05:04] HAZEL: Then I definitely won't waste time looking for an editorial.

[05:08] TOM: In the end, I selected a human interest story about a seriously ill young girl. A large group of people, most of them strangers, raised money for her to receive treatment abroad. Some papers focused only on everyone's generosity, while others asked the wider question of why the treatment was unavailable here.

[05:30] HAZEL: Stories like that usually affect me very strongly, so I'll avoid human interest pieces. I might choose something in the arts, perhaps contrasting film reviews or looking at arts funding. I haven't decided yet.
[05:46] TOM: That could work well.
[05:48] HAZEL: Thanks, Tom. Your advice has been extremely helpful.
[05:52] TOM: You're welcome. Good luck with the assignment.
[05:58] NARRATOR: That is the end of part three. You now have one minute to check your answers to part three.

passages.title: Early History Of Keeping Clean
content: 📌 Early history of keeping clean

Prehistoric times
• water was used to rinse [ _____ ] from the hands

Ancient Babylon
• a soap-like substance was made in [ _____ ] cylinders

Ancient Greece
• people cleaned their bodies with sand and similar materials
• a strigil was a scraper made of [ _____ ]
• clothing was washed in streams

Ancient Germany and Gaul
• soap was used to colour people’s [ _____ ]

Ancient Rome
• rain mixed animal fat, ash and clay into a useful laundry substance
• from about 312 BC, aqueducts carried water to Roman [ _____ ]

Europe in the Middle Ages
• reduced bathing helped outbreaks of [ _____ ] to spread
• makers began adding [ _____ ] to soap

Europe from the seventeenth century
• during the 1600s, bathing and cleanliness became more usual
• in 1791, Leblanc developed a method of producing soda ash from [ _____ ]
• in the early 1800s, Chevreul made soapmaking a [ _____ ]
• from the nineteenth century, soap was no longer subject to a [ _____ ]
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a lecture about the early history of personal cleanliness and soap. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Today, products for bathing, washing clothes, cleaning dishes and maintaining the home are ordinary parts of daily life.

[01:04] AUDIO: Yet the wide range we rely on is largely a modern development, dating mainly from the 20th century. The story of cleanliness begins much earlier. Prehistoric communities generally settled near water because it was essential for survival, and they soon recognized one simple cleansing effect. Water could rinse mud from their hands.

[01:29] AUDIO: Evidence from ancient Babylon shows that people understood a form of soapmaking by about 2800 BC. Archaeologists found clay cylinders whose inscriptions describe boiling fats together with ashes. Although this resembles a soap recipe, the cylinders do not explain what the substance was used for. The ancient Greeks bathed mainly for appearance and apparently did not wash with soap.

[02:00] AUDIO: They rubbed their bodies with sand, pumice or ash, applied oil and then removed the mixture of oil and dirt with a metal scraper called a stridgil. Their clothes were washed in streams without soap. In ancient Germany and Gaul, people also made a soap-like mixture from melted animal fat and ash. Instead of using it chiefly for washing, however, they used it to colour their hair red.

[02:30] AUDIO: A Roman legend links the name soap with Mount Sappo. Animal sacrifices supposedly left fat on the ground there, and rain carried this fat and wood ash into clay beside the river Tiber. Women discovered that the resulting mixture made washing clothes much easier. As Roman society developed, public bathing expanded too.

[02:55] AUDIO: Around 312 BC, aqueducts began supplying water to the famous Roman baths. Bathing became highly popular, and by the second century AD, the physician Galen was recommending soap for both cleaning and medical purposes. After Rome fell in 467 AD, bathing declined across much of Europe. Poor personal hygiene and unsanitary living conditions contributed to repeated outbreaks of disease during the Middle Ages, most famously the Black Death in the 14th century.

[03:33] AUDIO: Even so, soap-making became a recognised European craft. Guilds protected their methods, and makers combined plant or animal oils with ash. Perfume also began to be added, and specialised soaps gradually appeared for shaving, washing hair, bathing and laundering. A crucial advance towards mass production came in 1791.

[04:00] AUDIO: The French chemist Nicolas LeBlanc patented an economical process for converting salt into soda ash, the alkali that reacts with fat, to produce soap. His method supplied large quantities of reliable, inexpensive soda ash. About 20 years later, another French chemist, Michel Eugène Chevreau, explained the chemical relationships among fats, glycerine and fatty acids. His research established the scientific basis of fat and soap chemistry, turning soap-making from a craft into a science.

[04:40] AUDIO: Further 19th century improvements made production cheaper and easier. Soap had long been treated as a luxury, and was heavily taxed in several countries. When this tax disappeared in the 19th century, ordinary people could afford soap more readily, and standards of cleanliness rose. Its wider use then encouraged the development of gentler bathing soaps and products suitable for the washing machines available by the start of the 20th century.
[05:14] AUDIO: That is the end of part four. You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.

content: 📌 Customer satisfaction survey
Customer details
Name: Sophie BirdOccupation: [ _____ ]Purpose of today’s trip: [ _____ ]
Journey information
Return station: [ _____ ]Ticket type: standard [ _____ ] ticketTicket price: £ [ _____ ]Date purchased: yesterdayPlace of purchase: [ _____ ]
Satisfaction with the journey
Most satisfied with: the wifiLeast satisfied with: the [ _____ ] this morning
Satisfaction with station facilities
Most satisfied with: the amount of [ _____ ] providedLeast satisfied with: the shortage of seating, especially on the [ _____ ]Neither satisfied nor dissatisfied with: the [ _____ ]
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: Part one. You will hear a railway representative conducting a customer satisfaction survey with a passenger. First, you have some time to look at questions one to six. Now listen carefully and answer questions one to six.
[00:55] MAN: Hello. Would you be willing to answer a few questions about the journey you made today? We're carrying out a customer satisfaction survey.
[01:07] SOPHIE: Yes, that's fine. I have around ten minutes before my train home and I've only come for the day.
[01:14] MAN: Excellent. Thank you. Could I start by taking your name?
[01:20] SOPHIE: Sophie Bird.
[01:22] MAN: Thanks. And what is your occupation if you don't mind me asking?
[01:28] SOPHIE: I work as a journalist.
[01:31] MAN: That sounds interesting.
[01:33] SOPHIE: It usually is.
[01:35] MAN: Did you travel here for work today?
[01:37] SOPHIE: No, today is actually my day off. The reason I came was to do some shopping.
[01:44] MAN: I see.
[01:45] SOPHIE: I do make the same journey for work occasionally though.
[01:49] MAN: Right. I'd like to record a few details about today's journey now.
[01:55] SOPHIE: Of course.
[01:57] MAN: Which station will you be returning to?
[02:01] SOPHIE: Staunfirth. That's where I live.
[02:04] MAN: Let me check the spelling: S-T-A-U-N-F-I-R-T-H?
[02:17] SOPHIE: That's correct.
[02:18] MAN: And that was also the station you travelled from this morning?
[02:22] SOPHIE: Yes.
[02:24] MAN: What sort of ticket did you purchase? I'm guessing it wasn't a season ticket, since this isn't a daily trip.

[02:33] SOPHIE: No, I bought an ordinary return ticket. It was the standard fare because I don't have a rail card, so there was no discount. I really should get one because it would reduce the price considerably.
[02:49] MAN: You would have saved 20% today. How much did the ticket cost?
[02:54] SOPHIE: It was £23.70. Would you say that represents good value? Not especially. It feels expensive for a journey lasting only 45 minutes.
[03:08] MAN: That's a common complaint. I take it you didn't book a long time in advance?
[03:15] SOPHIE: No. I know fares are lower if you buy a week beforehand, but I hadn't decided to come at that point.
[03:23] MAN: So did you purchase it this morning?
[03:26] SOPHIE: No, I bought it yesterday.
[03:28] MAN: Do you normally get your tickets at the station?

[03:32] SOPHIE: Usually, yes. But the ticket office shuts early, and I dislike the machines. There is often a cue, and the machines are sometimes out of service. The office ought to remain open longer.
[03:48] MAN: We've heard similar comments from quite a few passengers.
[03:52] SOPHIE: So, to answer the question, I purchased an electronic ticket online.
[04:01] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the survey, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10. Now listen, and answer questions 7 to 10.
[04:45] MAN: Thank you. Let's move on to how satisfied you were with the journey. What pleased you most today?
[04:53] SOPHIE: The Wi-Fi was the best feature. It has improved a great deal and makes working on the train much easier when I need to.
[05:04] MAN: You're the first respondent today to mention that. It's useful to hear something positive. Was there anything about the journey that disappointed you?
[05:16] SOPHIE: The service is normally reliable, and the trains generally arrive on schedule. This morning, however, there was a delay of roughly 15 minutes.
[05:27] MAN: I'll note that. I'd also like your opinion of the station facilities. The station has recently been upgraded. Which improvement satisfies you most?

[05:40] SOPHIE: The amount of information provided about departure times is much better. Everything is clearer now. Previously, there was only one display board, which was hard to see, and that was frustrating.
[05:56] MAN: Good. Is there any facility you are dissatisfied with?
[06:01] SOPHIE: Overall, the station is much better. The trains are newer, and the new cafe is pleasant. But there still aren't enough seats, particularly on the platforms.
[06:14] MAN: So I should record seating as the feature you're least satisfied with?
[06:19] SOPHIE: Yes, that's right.
[06:21] MAN: Finally, I'll name a few other facilities. Please say whether you are satisfied, dissatisfied, or neither.
[06:31] SOPHIE: All right.
[06:32] MAN: What is your view of the station parking?
[06:36] SOPHIE: Honestly, I don't have an opinion because I never use it.
[06:40] MAN: In that case, I'll mark parking as neither satisfactory nor unsatisfactory.
[06:47] SOPHIE: Yes, I suppose that's accurate.
[06:51] MAN: Right. And how about…
[06:57] NARRATOR: That is the end of part one. You now have one minute to check your answers to part one.

transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear the chair of a local council committee describing recent changes to a public park. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 16. As chair of the council committee responsible for public spaces, I want to explain the latest improvements at Croft Valley Park.

[00:59] AUDIO: Please look at the plan you were given. The overall layout is familiar. There are entrances at the north and south with the lake occupying the centre. The cafe remains where it has always been.

[01:15] AUDIO: It faces the water and stands immediately beside the old museum. The toilets are less conveniently placed. We intend to move them towards the middle of the grounds because at present they are in the far north eastern corner close to the adventure playground. The formal gardens have been planted again and should look their best within the next couple of months.

[01:41] AUDIO: Previously they were behind the old museum. Their new site is near the south entrance in the strip between the park boundary and the path running north past the lake towards the museum. Another new feature is an outdoor gym that both adults and children can use. It is beside the glass houses on the eastern side of the path leading in from the south gate.

[02:08] AUDIO: The equipment is among the trees so it is easy to miss. The skateboard ramp has also been a real success and is especially busy after school and during holidays. You will find it near the old museum at the end of the short western branch that leaves the main path between the lake and the museum. We have also created a wildflower area to encourage bees and butterflies.

[02:39] AUDIO: It lies on the curve of the path along the lake's eastern side, a little south of the adventure playground. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 17 to 20. I will now give you some more detail about two of the park's facilities.

[03:36] AUDIO: The adventure playground is one of our most exciting additions. We realised there was nowhere suitable for children to use their energy so the available budget was used to build a completely new play area in a large section at the northern end of the park. It stays open throughout the year, although closing time is earlier in winter and nobody has to pay to enter. Children of every age may choose any activity but an adult must remain with them.

[04:10] AUDIO: Seating is provided so parents can supervise while taking a rest. Finally, I should mention the glass houses. Considerable work was needed after a serious fire destroyed much of their western side, more than £80,000 paid for replacement glass, metal supports and plants. However, the tropical palm collection was too costly to restore and is still missing.

[04:42] AUDIO: The buildings currently open from 10 in the morning until 3 in the afternoon, Monday through Thursday, and we hope weekend opening will begin soon. Many local people supported the restoration by giving either money or their time. The gardens have... That is the end of part two.
[05:05] AUDIO: You now have one minute to check your answers to part two.

content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 3: "Presentation About Refrigeration"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: Part 3. You will hear two students, Annie and Jack, discussing a presentation about refrigeration. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24.
[00:54] ANNIE: Alright, Jack. Before we work out the structure of our refrigeration presentation, shall we compare the information we've found so far?
[01:03] JACK: Sure, although to be honest, I haven't managed to research very much yet.

[01:09] ANNIE: Neither have I, but I did read a useful piece about ice houses. I'd already come across examples from the 18th and 19th centuries in Britain, so I knew they were generally placed underground or in a shaded spot, often near a lake that froze in winter. People cut the ice into blocks and put them inside. What was new to me was that straw or sawdust acted as insulation, allowing the ice to remain frozen for several months.
[01:42] ANNIE: The Romans had their own form of refrigeration as well.
[01:46] JACK: Really? I had no idea.

[01:48] ANNIE: They dug deep pits and brought in snow from mountain areas, even though those mountains were quite far away. The snow went into the pits and ice developed underneath it. Afterwards, both products were sold. Ice was more expensive than snow, so I imagine it was mainly rich people who could buy it.
[02:10] JACK: That seems likely. I found something on present-day household refrigerators. Apparently, they used several kinds of technology, but the technical explanations were beyond me.
[02:22] ANNIE: It also makes you think about where old fridges end up once owners replace them.
[02:29] JACK: Are you thinking of the environmental damage caused by the gases inside them?
[02:34] ANNIE: Exactly. There are organizations that can recover most parts without causing harm, but some owners still abandon unwanted fridges in rural areas.
[02:45] JACK: Unfortunately, preventing that is difficult. Altogether, about three million are thrown away in the UK each year.
[02:53] ANNIE: That figure is surprising, given that refrigerators rarely stop working.

[02:59] JACK: I agree. Here, a domestic fridge is used for around 11 years on average, and many continue for 20 years or longer. If you spread the purchase price over that length of time, it costs relatively little compared with several other home appliances.
[03:17] ANNIE: That's true. Manufacturers probably persuade customers to pay extra by offering different finishes and styles. When my parents bought their first one, I doubt there was much choice.
[03:30] JACK: No, the market has certainly changed.

[05:42] ANNIE: Perhaps that could be yours.

[06:18] JACK: Fair enough. I'll deal with that one.

[06:45] JACK: Should domestic refrigerators have a section of their own? They're familiar to practically everyone.

passages.title: How The Industrial Revolution Affected Life In Britain
content: 📌 How the Industrial Revolution affected life in Britain

19th century
• A nation’s [ _____ ] was judged partly by what its citizens owned.
• Advances in the production of goods and in [ _____ ] transformed everyday life.
Main areas of change

Manufacturing
• The Revolution depended on newly available forms of [ _____ ].
• The leading sector was [ _____ ], whose products became widely accessible.
• The arrival of large [ _____ ] required factories and encouraged migration to towns.

Transport
• Railways eventually replaced canals as the principal network.
• The new system changed shopping habits:
  • wider circulation of [ _____ ] showed people what shops were selling;
  • customers were no longer restricted to [ _____ ] products.

Retailing
• The first department stores opened.
• Products could be seen more clearly:
  • inside shops because of improved [ _____ ];
  • from the street because shop [ _____ ] became larger.
• Persuasive [ _____ ] became far more widespread.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear part of a lecture about how the Industrial Revolution changed everyday life in Britain. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Hello, everyone.

[00:52] AUDIO: Today, I'm going to present the research I carried out into Britain's social history during the Industrial Revolution, with particular attention to the way ordinary people's lives were altered. This period introduced a new pattern of behavior, consumerism, in which buying and selling products became central to daily life. During the 19th century, for the first time, the amount and standard of what people owned came to be treated as evidence of Britain's wealth. Earlier generations had possessed very little, but the Industrial Revolution changed that situation.

[01:34] AUDIO: Between the middle of the 18th century and the end of the 19th, advances in the manufacture of goods, together with developments in technology, produced enormous social changes that touched almost everyone. Let's begin with manufacturing. Steam engines and coal are the images most people associate with the Industrial Revolution, and with good reason. Without these new sources of power, it could not have occurred.

[02:06] AUDIO: They replaced the water mills and windmills that had previously supplied most energy. For much of the 19th century, textiles formed the most advanced industry. As a result, fashionable cloth, lace, and ribbons became affordable and widely available. Before industrialization, goods for sale were generally produced in small workshops, often inside people's homes.

[02:36] AUDIO: Then, extremely large machines were developed that could manufacture items more quickly and in far greater quantities. Because those machines needed much more room, factories were constructed and gradually took the place of workshops. Workers now had to travel to their jobs, and large populations moved from rural villages into towns. Manufacturing was not the only driver of consumerism.

[03:09] AUDIO: Transport technology also changed dramatically. The 18th century's slow horse-drawn coaches and carts, which carried only small loads along rough roads, were followed by an extensive canal network that was especially useful for freight. Canals later declined as the railway system expanded and became the main means of carrying both people and products across the country. Trains transported coal, iron, and clothing, but also newspapers.

[03:44] AUDIO: These made thousands of readers better informed about national events and, importantly, about the goods offered in shops, which encouraged further spending. Faster transport also made distribution much more efficient, allowing products to be sold nationwide rather than only in a local market. Retailing was the third major area of change. Shops increased rapidly in both number and quality, and small businesses lost customers to the new department stores that appeared during the 19th century.

[04:24] AUDIO: Their owners developed new methods of stocking goods and attracting shoppers. Better lighting inside stores made displays much easier to see. From the street, plate glass allowed shop windows to be considerably larger than before, so more merchandise was visible. Promotion changed as well.

[04:46] AUDIO: Instead of simply announcing that an item was available, advertising increasingly tried to persuade people to shop. The historian Judith Flanders argues that one of the Industrial Revolution's most important consequences was the creation of choice. Products that had once been luxuries, such as sugar and cutlery, became ordinary conveniences and then necessities. Soon, living without them seemed impossible, rather like mobile phones today.
[05:24] AUDIO: That is the end of part four. You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.
